De Stijl. The name means The Style, and it was a Dutch art movement from nineteen seventeen to nineteen thirty one that pursued universal harmony through pure geometric abstraction. It reduced form to primary colors—red, yellow, blue—along with black lines and white space. Founded by Piet Mondrian and Theo van Doesburg, De Stijl applied rationalist principles across painting, sculpture, architecture, and design, seeking timeless, impersonal beauty as a bridge between art and everyday life.

The movement was founded in nineteen seventeen in the Netherlands during World War I. The journal De Stijl, also founded that year, became the movement's publication and intellectual nexus, distributing ideas across Europe. Piet Mondrian's mature abstract paintings defined the visual language. Grids of black lines dividing fields of primary color and white became iconic representations of what pure abstraction could mean.

The aesthetic principles were systematic and rigorous. The elimination of all curved lines. Reduction to primary colors plus black, white, and gray. Asymmetrical balance. Mondrian believed that geometric abstraction expressed universal truth, that this visual language could transcend culture and individual taste, creating what he thought of as a visual Esperanto accessible to all humans regardless of background or nationality.

De Stijl extended far beyond painting into architecture and furniture design through Gerrit Rietveld. His Utrecht Chair and the Rietveld Schröder House made it a total design philosophy, not merely a painting movement. Every aspect of living space could be rethought through geometric principles.

But the movement dissolved in the early nineteen thirties as fascism rose and its utopian vision faltered. Mondrian emigrated to Paris and later New York, continuing his abstract practice throughout his life while De Stijl as an organized collective faded away.
